title: Direct Brow Lift -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Brow ptosis, the downward migration of periorbital soft tissues, is a common occurrence that steadily increases in individuals who are 50 and older. This condition may pose functional and cosmetic concerns for the patient. Depending on the severity, those affected may complain of issues such as visual field obstruction or an unappealing resting facial aesthetic. Several surgical and nonsurgical techniques have been developed to manage this age-related process. One of these procedures is the direct brow lift. Clinicians specializing in facial rejuvenation techniques should thoroughly understand the medical and surgical management of brow ptosis. These techniques can help avoid complications, optimize the results, and better achieve the patient's goals.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Course participants gain an in-depth understanding of brow ptosis, its prevalence, and its impact on patients' functional and cosmetic well-being, particularly those who are 50 and older. The focus is on the direct brow lift procedure, exploring its nuances, indications, and potential outcomes. The complexities of patient evaluation, surgical techniques, and postoperative care specific to periorbital aging are discussed. The course emphasizes the collaborative nature of addressing periorbital aging through the direct brow lift. The significance of an interprofessional team, including surgeons, nurses, anesthesiologists, and rehabilitation specialists, is emphasized. Collaborative learning experiences are highlighted to enhance competence in patient assessment, preoperative planning, intraoperative execution, and postoperative care.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Introduction
content: The periorbital region, including the eyebrows, upper eyelids, and lower eyelids, undergoes predictable changes during aging. [1] With advancing age, the brow descends relative to the supraorbital rim, often resulting in dermatochalasis. Commonly, this presents as hooding of the lateral eyelids, but, in severe cases, may result in upper visual field obstruction. [2] Other less common causes of brow ptosis include facial paralysis and posttraumatic deformity. Various surgical options exist to reposition the brow, ranging from traditional open techniques to newer endoscopic approaches. Each method has strengths and weaknesses, but no procedure has been proven superior in all clinical scenarios. [3]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Introduction
content: In recent years, the focus of aesthetic surgery has shifted toward minimally invasive techniques, such as endoscopic browlifting. [4] However, performing traditional open approaches is still essential for facial surgeons as these techniques offer the highest precision when repositioning the brow. This activity discusses the details of one such open approach, the direct brow lift, and its significance in rejuvenating the upper third of the face.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The upper third of the face exhibits many characteristic signs of aging, including: Horizontal midforehead lines, due to the vertical action of the frontalis muscle Fullness of the upper lateral eyelid, caused by the descent of the upper facial soft tissues and brow ptosis Vertical and oblique glabellar lines from the action of the corrugator supercilii and the depressor supercilii (ie, superomedial orbicularis oculi) muscles Horizontal glabellar and nasal root lines, due to the action of the procerus muscle [5]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Pertinent Anatomic Structures
content: Layers of the forehead The skin of the brow is thicker than that of the upper eyelid. The thickest part of the brow skin is towards the middle, near the glabella, which is highly sebaceous. Skin with high sebum secretion is more prone to scarring; therefore, most surgeons attempt to avoid making a direct brow incision in this area whenever feasible. Beneath the skin lies subdermal fat, and beneath that is the muscular layer. The most superficial muscle is the procerus, with the corrugator underneath and the frontalis beneath that. The corrugator is deepest medially, where it originates on the frontal bone, and most superficial laterally, where it inserts into the dermis of the brow. Below the muscle is the periosteum, which adheres to the underlying calvarium. [6]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Pertinent Anatomic Structures
content: Supratrochlear nerve This nerve provides sensory innervation to the medial upper eyelid, glabella, and a small portion of the conjunctiva. The supratrochlear nerve courses through the corrugator muscle and is usually located 1 cm medial to the exit point of the supraorbital nerve or 1.7 cm lateral to the midline. [7]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Pertinent Anatomic Structures
content: Supraorbital nerve This nerve exits a notch or foramen roughly 2.7 cm lateral to the midline forehead between the midpupillary line and the medial limbus. The supraorbital nerve further divides into deep and superficial branches, providing sensory innervation to the frontoparietal and upper eyelid skin, respectively. [7]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Pertinent Anatomic Structures
content: Frontal branch of cranial nerve VII, the facial nerve This provides motor innervation to the forehead muscles (frontalis, corrugator supercilii, procerus) and the upper orbicularis oculi muscle. The path of this nerve may be approximated by the Pitanguy line, which is drawn from a point 0.5 cm inferior to the tragus to a point 1.5 cm superior to the lateral brow (see Image. Temporal Branch Course). [8]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Ideal Brow Location and Shape
content: In the classical ideal of women's brow position, the brow forms an arch, with its highest point located above the supraorbital rim, between the lateral limbus and the lateral canthus. The eyebrow should possess a defined and thicker appearance in the medial region, aligning with or just above the supraorbital rim. The brow should ascend above the rim, moving laterally and gradually tapering for a harmonious aesthetic. In men, the ideal brow is relatively flat and lies at the level of the supraorbital rim.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Indications -- Indications for Any Brow Lift Surgery
content: Visual field obstruction Pseudoblepharoptosis (excess upper eyelid skin prolapses over the lash line, but no pathology of the eyelid musculature or levator aponeurosis is present—most often due to significant dermatochalasis that is exacerbated by brow ptosis) Brow ptosis Facial paralysis Brow asymmetry (often due to unilateral or asymmetric blepharoptosis) Deep forehead rhytids (ie, wrinkles) Glabellar lines Concerns regarding the perceived resting facial aesthetic (eg, an angry or tired look) [9]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Indications -- Clinical Situations Favoring a Direct Brow Lift Approach
content: Lack of forehead rhytids Unilateral facial paralysis (provides precise control of the elevation of each brow individually) Convex forehead craniofacial skeleton (limits endoscopic approach) Receding hairline or baldness Heavy eyebrows Prior eyebrow scar Patient preference [10]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Indications -- Other Brow Lift Approaches
content: Endoscopic brow lift Consists of multiple small incisions made within the frontal and temporal hairlines to permit the insertion of the endoscope and surgical instruments [4] [12] Minimally invasive approach with a theoretically decreased risk of injury to neurovascular structures and shorter healing times Poorly suited for patients with receding hairlines or convex foreheads, which may restrict endoscopic visualization Requires fixation, typically with absorbable materials (eg, bioabsorbable anchors or sutures), to reposition and stabilize the forehead's soft tissues Only provides moderate brow elevation (several millimeters) [13]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Indications -- Other Brow Lift Approaches
content: Coronal brow lift Incision made several centimeters behind the hairline Incision is completely hidden within the hair Should be avoided in patients with elongated foreheads because this technique will elevate the patient's existing hairline Avoid this procedure in bald patients, as this may leave an unsightly scar

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Contraindications -- Contraindications to Brow Lift Surgery
content: The contraindications to any brow lift surgery include: Body dysmorphic disorder History of blepharoplasty, especially recent (because the brow lift is more likely to cause lagophthalmos in these cases) Dry eye syndrome or history of decreased tear production (also due to risk of lagophthalmos and worsened xerophthalmia) [17]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Personnel
content: The personnel included in the direct brow lift should consist of the following: Surgeon Surgical scrub technician Operating room nurse (circulator) An anesthesiologist or nurse anesthetist Notably, the procedure can be performed under local anesthesia, as preferred by the surgeon and patient.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Preparation
content: The patient should undergo a preoperative evaluation by a medical professional to assess surgical risk and optimize for general anesthesia, if required. A thorough physical examination should be conducted with the patient in an upright position, focusing on brow position, visual fields, rhytids, scars, and facial nerve function. To accurately assess brow position at rest, the patient should be instructed to close their eyes and fully relax the forehead, as many individuals with significant brow ptosis involuntarily contract the frontalis muscle when their eyes are open.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Preparation
content: Preoperative photographs are essential and should include frontal views in repose and with eyebrows elevated, as well as profile views in repose. If a concurrent blepharoplasty is planned, additional photographic views should be obtained. Patients should be counseled thoroughly about the procedure’s risks, benefits, and alternatives. Specific risks associated with a brow lift include improper brow position or asymmetry, incomplete eye closure, dry eyes, unsightly scarring, the need for revision surgery, alopecia, paresthesia, and facial nerve injury. Common surgical risks such as pain, bleeding, and infection should also be discussed.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Preparation
content: Setting realistic expectations is critical. Patients should be informed that while direct brow lifting and other facial rejuvenation procedures can create a more youthful appearance, the aging process will continue to occur. For instance, if the procedure offers a 10-year rejuvenation to a 60-year-old patient, the patient may appear 50 shortly after surgery, but will look 60 again by age 70, and 70 by age 80. Patients may be advised to take the herbal supplement Arnica montana during the perioperative period to reduce ecchymosis and edema. [18]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Preparation
content: Candidates for simultaneous facial rejuvenation procedures, such as blepharoplasty, fat transfer, or laser resurfacing, should be identified and counseled appropriately. Important anatomical landmarks must be carefully noted, including the supraorbital rim, supraorbital and supratrochlear neurovascular bundles, temporal line, sentinel vein, corrugator supercilii and procerus muscles, Pitanguy line, hairline position, and the desired brow shape and position. [1]

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Preparation
content: While general anesthesia may be used, it is not mandatory for all procedures. Muscle paralytics are typically avoided to facilitate intraoperative facial nerve monitoring if desired. A single preoperative dose of intravenous antibiotics targeting skin flora may be administered. The procedure is usually performed with the patient in the supine position. Skin marking begins with a fusiform beveled incision within the superior row of eyebrow hair. The upper incision is designed to match the desired amount of brow elevation, with most of the lift focused laterally to restore the natural brow contour.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Technique or Treatment
content: The patient is positioned and draped in a standard sterile fashion. A safety checklist is followed, and a surgical time-out is observed.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Technique or Treatment
content: The planned amount of skin to be resected is verified and compared to the preoperative markings. Local anesthesia (1% lidocaine with 1 to 100,000 epinephrine with a maximum of 7 mg/kg of lidocaine) is injected into the planned surgical site. Suppose the patient is undergoing the procedure awake. In that case, adding 8.4% bicarbonate to the local anesthetic (10% of the volume of the lidocaine) will buffer the local anesthetic and reduce discomfort during injection.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Technique or Treatment
content: A #15 blade scalpel creates a slightly beveled incision, allowing the final closure to naturally evert the skin edges (see Image. Direct Brow Lift). One should bevel the blade toward the hair follicle near the eyebrow to preserve the brow hairline.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Technique or Treatment
content: The skin and underlying soft tissue are resected while avoiding injury to underlying neurovascular structures and muscles (frontal and orbicularis oculi).
contents: Direct Brow Lift -- Technique or Treatment. The skin and underlying soft tissue are resected while avoiding injury to underlying neurovascular structures and muscles (frontal and orbicularis oculi).

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Technique or Treatment
content: The ptotic frontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles may be suspended to a more youthful position by superiorly anchoring them to the forehead periosteum. If prominent rhytids of the corrugator and procerus muscles need to be addressed, medial dissection may allow for sectioning these muscles.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Technique or Treatment
content: Hemostasis is achieved using pressure and limited electrocautery to avoid injury to the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Technique or Treatment
content: The deep layer of the wound is closed using absorbable sutures, commonly 4-0 or 5-0 poliglecaprone. The skin may then be closed using a 5-0 subcuticular or a running 6-0 cutaneous stitch using plain gut or polypropylene sutures.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Complications
content: Although rare, complications may include: Wound infections Hematoma Brow asymmetry Forehead paresthesias Injury to the frontal branch of the facial nerve Unsightly scar formation Alopecia of the eyebrow Need for revision Overcorrection Eye dryness [19] The meticulous surgical technique will minimize the appearance of the inevitable postoperative scar, particularly if the excision does not extend into the sebaceous skin of the glabella.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Clinical Significance
content: The direct brow lift represents an essential tool in the armamentarium of the aesthetic and reconstructive facial surgeon. Direct brow lifting provides precise repositioning of an asymmetric or ptotic brow, making it applicable in facial aging and facial paralysis. [20] The surgeon offering this technique should also be well-versed in the other approaches to brow lifting to advise and select the best plan for the individual patient. The outcomes can be very satisfactory in the hands of a knowledgeable and experienced surgeon.

title: Direct Brow Lift -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Recovery following direct brow lift surgery varies for each patient due to their individual functional and nutritional status. Meticulous local wound care ensures a healthy and clean healing environment. Blood thinners may be restarted on postoperative day 1. The patient should be counseled to avoid heavy lifting or straining until follow-up, to minimize edema and ecchymosis. When proper sterile technique is employed, postoperative antibiotics are not necessary. If used, permanent sutures for skin closure should be removed within 5 to 7 days, depending on the amount of wound tension present. Following surgery, the patient is typically seen regularly in the outpatient clinic until satisfactory healing has occurred.
